Per-Unit and Synchronous Reactance (Ch8, part 1)

Why this matters in the exam: Q4 of every exam is “Per-Unit and Synchronous Machines” (20 marks). Ch8 numericals fill Q4a and Q4b, worth 12 to 15 marks. Q4c is short answers. Both past papers open Q4 the same way. Jun23 Q4a (5 marks) asks for in ohms from OC/SC test results, then the per-unit and for a given P and Q. Jun24 Q4a (5 marks) asks for in per-unit from the tests, then and for a given P and pf. Ch8 has never been in a test or quiz, and the course files give only numerical answers for it. This pack sets out the method in full. The power angle, , excitation (V-curve) control and synchronous-motor PFC are in pack M11.

1. The core ideas

1.1 What per-unit is (Lecture 8.3.1–8.3.2)

  • What it is: a dimensionless ratio. You still write “pu” after it. 0.83 pu means 83% of base.
  • When to use it: always for synchronous machines. The course says they are “normally analysed in per-unit” (Lecture 8.3.8).
  • The four-step procedure (Lecture 8.3.2): (1) work out the base values; (2) divide every given quantity by its base; (3) solve the circuit in pu; (4) multiply the answers by their bases.
  • Trap: the choice of base does not change the final answer in real units. It only changes the pu numbers. If you get different real answers with different bases, you have made an error.

1.2 Choosing the bases (Lecture 8.3.5, 8.3.8; formula sheet section 8)

You choose two primary bases. Everything else is derived from them.

  • Trap: uses the line voltage and the total VA. Mixing phase voltage with total VA gives a value 3 times too small. The two mistakes cancel only if you use both phase quantities: .

1.3 Line vs phase, total vs per-phase (Lecture 8.3.4, 8.3.7)

This is the big advantage of per-unit:

  • The pu value of a line voltage equals the pu value of the phase voltage. For example, 18 kV line on a 16 kV base is 1.125 pu, and kV phase on a kV base is also 1.125 pu.
  • The pu value of per-phase power equals the pu value of total power.
  • So in pu there are no or 3 factors. The 3ph equation becomes simply pu.
Real units (3ph, star) Per-unit
(phase volts)
  • Trap: the comes back only when you convert to real units. Multiply a pu voltage by the line base to get a line voltage (Q8.11 hint). Multiply a pu current by , which already contains the .

1.4 How a synchronous machine works (Lecture 8.1.2, 8.2.2, 8.2.4)

  • Stator: a standard 3ph AC winding, as in the induction machine. Balanced 3ph currents make a field rotating at (p = pole-pairs; ).
  • Rotor: either permanent magnets, or a field winding fed with DC field current (excitation) through slip rings. This rotor field is fixed relative to the rotor, so it rotates with the rotor.
  • The two fields want to align. So the rotor turns at exactly synchronous speed, with no slip.
  • Turning the excited rotor induces 3ph voltages in the stator. is proportional to speed and to (until the iron saturates). Its frequency is set by the speed.
  • Rotor angle is the angle by which the rotor field leads the stator field. In the circuit it is the angle of relative to . means generating. means motoring. means no load.
  • Two control knobs (Lecture 8.5.1): sets and so the reactive power Q. The rotor angle sets the real power P. (Details are in M11.)

1.5 The per-phase equivalent circuit and the sign convention (Lecture 8.4.2)

The course draws the round-rotor machine as a source behind the synchronous impedance , with the current flowing out of the machine towards the terminals . This is the generator convention:

  • is the stator winding resistance. is the synchronous reactance, from the inductance of the stator winding. Normally , so is highly inductive. is often neglected.
  • is the reference: .
  • is in phase with . leads by .
  • The only loss in the model is .

Motor vs generator. The course gives only this one equation. Its slides show motoring as the same circuit with (Lecture 8.2.2, 8.4.6). There are two equivalent ways to handle a motor:

Both give the same (Worked Example 4 shows this). Say which convention you are using, and draw the current arrow on your circuit.

  • Trap: using with a motor’s input current. That gives the wrong (wrong sign of and the wrong magnitude).

Drag δ down through zero and on to negative values: P changes sign as the machine goes from generating to motoring. Then move E0 above and below 1 pu to see Q change sign.

1.6 Finding from the open- and short-circuit tests (Lecture 8.5.2–8.5.4)

The SC curve does not saturate because the stator field nearly cancels the rotor field, so the net flux is small.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Using the OC line voltage as if it were a phase voltage. . Jun23 gives 3.676 Ω. Forgetting gives 6.37 Ω.
  • Answering in the wrong units. Jun23 Q4a(i) asks for ohms (“not per-unit”). Jun24 Q4a(i) asks for per-unit. Read the question twice.
  • Computing with mixed bases, such as phase voltage with total VA. Use every time.
  • Using V = 1 pu when the question says “5% above rated”. Then , not .
  • Wrong sign on the current angle. A generator at lagging pf, or delivering Q, has lagging (negative angle). Jun23 Q4a(ii) is , not .
  • Treating MW as MVA. “Delivering 200 MW at 0.8 pf” means MVA = 0.625 pu, not 0.5 pu.
  • Putting into pu equations. In pu, and . The appears only in and when you convert a pu voltage back to phase volts.
  • Motor sign error. With the input current , use . Draw the arrow before you write the equation.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

PER-UNIT (Ch8.3)        pu = actual / base      choice of base never changes real answer
 Primary:   S_B = rating (total 3ph VA),  V_B = rated LINE voltage
 Derived:   I_B = S_B / (sqrt3 V_B)   [1ph: S_B/V_B]
            Z_B = R_B = X_B = V_B^2 / S_B      P_B = Q_B = S_B
 In pu:     line V pu = phase V pu; total S pu = phase S pu; NO sqrt3 or 3
            S = V I*,  P = V I cos(phi)
 Back:      V_line = V(pu) x V_B ;  I(A) = I(pu) x I_B ;  Z(ohm) = Z(pu) x Z_B

SYNC MACHINE MODEL (Ch8.4)   I out of machine (generator convention)
 E0 = V + I (R + jXs)          V = V<0 reference ; delta = angle of E0
 Motor (I_m into machine): E0 = V - I_m (R + jXs) ; delta < 0
 Field current IF sets E0 (and Q); rotor angle sets P  (see M11)

Xs FROM TESTS (Ch8.5) - SAME IF for both readings
 |Zs| = (V_OC,line / sqrt3) / I_SC        Xs = sqrt(|Zs|^2 - R^2)
 Xs(pu) = Xs / Z_B           slopes: use IF = 1 A
 IF for E0 = 1 pu (synchronisation) = IF_test x V_B / V_OC
 IF = E0(pu) x IF(E0 = 1 pu)    (unsaturated)

V and I FROM LOAD
 V = V<0 pu (1.05 = 5% above, 0.97 = 3% below)
 S = P/pf  or sqrt(P^2+Q^2)  (pu on machine rating)
 I = (S/V) < -acos(pf)  lag / delivering Q
 I = (S/V) < +acos(pf)  lead / absorbing Q      or  I = (S/V)*
 Check: MW is not MVA; use actual V in S/V; answer in ohms or pu as asked
